## User  <sub>2026-11-16T11:00:38.663Z</sub>

lets first chat about the porter stemmer, why does it mean a deleted word will still appear if there is text reconstruction?

## Assistant  <sub>2026-11-16T11:00:54.225Z</sub>

Reconstruction does remove the deleted word. My earlier wording made it sound like the deleted word itself shows up again, and it doesn't. The issue is narrower than that.

**How porter works:** it reduces words to a stem, both when text is indexed and when you search. "cats", "cat" and "catting" are all indexed as `cat`, and "running", "runs" and "run" as `run`. A search then matches on stems, not exact words.

**The edge case I meant:**
- Inside one session you type "the cat and the cats", then delete "cat", leaving "the and the cats".
- The reconstructed text correctly contains no "cat".
- But a search for `cat` still returns this session, because "cats" is indexed as `cat`.

So the deleted word never appears in the text or in the snippet. It's the remaining word "cats" that matches. A test that types a word, deletes it and searches for it only gets a wrong hit if a variant of the word is still in that session. That's rare, but possible.

**The broader trade-off:**

| | Porter stemming | Exact words (`unicode61` only) |
|---|---|---|
| `search "run"` | finds run, runs, running, runner | finds only "run" |
| Matches that surprise you | some: "university" and "universal" both become `univers` | none |
| Your spec ("every word must appear in the same session") | loosened to "a word with the same stem appears" | met literally |
| Hebrew | no effect (porter is English-only) | same |
| Case and accents | ignored | ignored |

I still recommend exact words, because results then match exactly what was written, and the spec's AND rule holds literally. But porter isn't wrong. It gives better recall for English prose, at the cost of some surprising matches. If you want some of that recall with exact words, there's a middle option: prefix search, where `run*` finds run, runs and running, but only when you add the `*`.

Which do you want: exact words, exact words plus `*` prefix search, or porter?

I'll set up `ai-logs/` at the very end, because this session's transcript keeps growing until then. Please paste the design chat's share link whenever you have it.

**About running `brain` as root**

For the sleep/wake test, the problem isn't `brain`'s permissions. `brain` never suspends the machine; it only notices a suspend and reopens the keyboards on wake. What needs root is the **test**: suspending and then waking the machine automatically with `rtcwake`. Running `brain` as root wouldn't change that. The same goes for later end-to-end tests that type through a virtual keyboard (`/dev/uinput`): the test needs root, not `brain`.

Running `brain` itself as root would also cause real problems:
1. **Security.** A keylogger running as root is the worst case if anything in it is ever exploited.
2. **Desktop integration breaks.** Focus, clipboard, screen lock and layout all come over your desktop session's D-Bus. A root process, and especially a system service that starts before you log in, doesn't have that connection. It would need a second, per-user helper process just to reach it.
3. **File ownership.** The data folder would belong to root, so `brain query` run as you couldn't read it without extra permission work.

**What I suggest instead:**
- **Service:** a **systemd user service**. It starts when you log in, restarts automatically if it crashes, runs as you with full desktop access, and needs no root. I'd add the unit file and a `make install-service` target, so it's `systemctl --user enable --now brain`.
- **Tests that need root:** grant root only for exactly those:
  - **Sleep/wake:** you run `! sudo rtcwake -m mem -s 20` once while I watch. Or add a sudoers rule letting your user run only `rtcwake` without a password, so I can run it myself, now and in later tests.
  - **Typing tests:** a udev rule giving the `input` group access to `/dev/uinput`. Then the stage-4 tests can type through a real virtual keyboard instead of the synthetic source. This means anything in the `input` group can inject keystrokes, which is the trade-off.

So which do you want: the systemd user service plus narrow test permissions (which ones), or `brain` as a root system service with a separate user-session helper for the desktop parts?

# Build `brain` and install it system-wide.
#
#   make                    build (release) and install to $(BINDIR)
#   make build              build only
#   make install-service    install + enable the systemd user service
#   make uninstall-service  stop, disable and remove the service
#   make uninstall          remove the installed binary
#
# cargo runs as you; only the copy uses sudo, so target/ never becomes
# root-owned and root needs no Rust toolchain.

PREFIX ?= /usr
BINDIR ?= $(PREFIX)/bin
BIN    := target/release/brain

.PHONY: all build install uninstall install-service uninstall-service

all: install

build:
	cargo build --release

install: build
	sudo install -m 0755 $(BIN) $(BINDIR)/brain

uninstall:
	sudo rm -f $(BINDIR)/brain

# The service runs as you (no root); see packaging/brain.service.
UNITDIR ?= $(HOME)/.config/systemd/user

install-service: install
	install -Dm 0644 packaging/brain.service $(UNITDIR)/brain.service
	systemctl --user daemon-reload
	systemctl --user enable --now brain.service

uninstall-service:
	-systemctl --user disable --now brain.service
	rm -f $(UNITDIR)/brain.service
	systemctl --user daemon-reload

## Assistant  <sub>2026-11-16T11:19:48.854Z</sub>

The service is built, tested and pushed. To finish the sleep/wake test I need you to run the root setup script once, because it needs your password:

```
! sudo sh scripts/setup-test-permissions.sh
```

What it installs:
- **`/etc/sudoers.d/brain-tests`**: your user may run exactly `sudo /usr/sbin/rtcwake -m mem -s 20` without a password. No other command, and no other arguments, are allowed. The file is checked with `visudo` before it's installed.
- **`/etc/udev/rules.d/70-brain-uinput.rules`**: the user logged in at this machine gets access to `/dev/uinput`, the virtual keyboard device. This is for the typing tests later.
- `sudo sh scripts/setup-test-permissions.sh --undo` removes both.

**After you run it,** I'll start a test `brain` and run the `rtcwake` command. The machine suspends and wakes by itself 20 s later, and the connection to this session will drop for that time. KDE locks the screen when it wakes (your lock-on-resume setting is the default, on), so you'll need to unlock it. Then type a few characters anywhere, and I'll check the log shows sleep, wake, the reopened keyboard and your keys.

**How the service works**
- **The unit file** (`packaging/brain.service`) is a systemd *user* unit:
  - It runs `/usr/bin/brain run --data-dir ~/brain-data` as you, inside your desktop session, so it has the session D-Bus that KWin focus, Klipper, screen lock and layouts need. Keyboards are read through your `input` group, so there's no root anywhere.
  - It starts with the Plasma session (`graphical-session.target`), after the compositor, and stops at logout.
  - On stop, systemd sends SIGTERM, so `brain` shuts down cleanly: final ingest, `stop` event, KWin script unloaded.
  - `Restart=on-failure` restarts it 5 s after a crash, at most 5 times in 2 minutes. `NoNewPrivileges` stops it from ever gaining privileges.
  - Its messages go to the journal: `journalctl --user -u brain -f`.
- **A code change for service mode:** a service can start before KWin is ready. Before, a failed first connection meant no focus tracking for the whole run. Now `brain` keeps its D-Bus connection and loads the focus script as soon as KWin appears. I haven't tested this case live, because that would mean restarting your compositor.
- **Installing:** `make install-service` builds and installs `/usr/bin/brain` (sudo for the copy only), puts the unit in `~/.config/systemd/user/`, and enables and starts it. `make uninstall-service` removes it.
- **Tested** with a temporary copy of the unit, pointed at the built binary and a throwaway folder, since removed:
  - It started with the keyboard and KWin focus, at 2.6 MB memory.
  - After `kill -9`, systemd restarted it within 5 s, and the new instance cleaned up the old KWin script.
  - `systemctl stop` exited cleanly.
- **Not done:** I haven't enabled the real service, because it would lock `~/brain-data` while you test by hand. When you want it on, run `make install-service`. Stop it (`systemctl --user stop brain`) before running `brain run` yourself on the same folder.

Sleep/wake now works and is tested. While testing it I also found and fixed a bug where an animated terminal title split sessions every second. Everything is committed and pushed (`22fcab1`).

## How it was done

**1. Service without root** (`packaging/brain.service`, `make install-service`)
- It's a systemd *user* unit. It runs `/usr/bin/brain run --data-dir ~/brain-data` as you, inside your Plasma session, because focus tracking, clipboard, screen lock and layouts all come from your session's D-Bus. Keyboards are read through your `input` group.
- It starts with the desktop session after KWin, stops at logout with SIGTERM (a clean `brain` shutdown), and restarts 5 s after a crash. Its messages go to `journalctl --user -u brain`.
- Code change: if KWin isn't up yet when `brain` starts, it now waits for KWin to appear on D-Bus and then attaches focus tracking. Before, it gave up for the whole run.
- Tested with a temporary copy of the unit, since removed:
  - It started with the keyboard and focus tracking.
  - After `kill -9`, systemd restarted it within 5 s, and the new instance unloaded the old KWin script.
  - A normal stop was clean.
- I haven't enabled the real service. Run `make install-service` when you want it on.

**2. Narrow test permissions** (`scripts/setup-test-permissions.sh`, which you ran)
- **Sudoers:** your user may run exactly one root command without a password: `rtcwake -m no -s 30`. It sets the wake alarm and nothing else. `visudo` checks the file before it's installed.
- **udev:** the user logged in at this machine may open `/dev/uinput`, for the future virtual-keyboard tests.
- `--undo` removes both.

**3. The sleep/wake test**
- **First attempt, a failed test design (my mistake):** `rtcwake -m mem` suspends without telling logind, so `brain` got no "going to sleep" or "woke up" signal and saw nothing. I changed the permission to "set the alarm only", which is why you ran the script a second time.
- **Second attempt, the real path:**
  - I set the alarm with `rtcwake`, then suspended with `systemctl suspend`. That's the same route the KDE menu or closing the lid takes.
  - `brain` logged `sleep`, then `lock` (keys dropped from there, so your unlock password wasn't captured), `wake`, `resumed: reopened 1 keyboard(s)` and `unlock`.
  - Then your typing was captured normally.
  - Your machine woke after about 2 s instead of 30. That's the hardware waking early, not `brain`.

**4. Bug found during the test**
- The terminal's title alternates `◐ Home assignment…` and `◑ Home assignment…` every second: Claude Code's spinner. Because sessions are keyed by window title, terminal typing was being split into a new session every second.
- Titles now have leading status symbols stripped: shapes, stars, spinner frames, and VS Code's unsaved dot. There's a test for it.

## Decisions and edge cases

* **The mouse is not captured.** `brain` reads keyboards only. A mouse
  click can move the text cursor, but its position on screen tells `brain`
  nothing about where in the text the cursor went, so reconstruction cannot
  use it. Tiers 0/1 (and tier 2) therefore **do not support text edited
  after the cursor was moved with the mouse** (clicking into the middle of a
  line to fix a typo, selecting with the mouse, drag and drop): typing
  continues from where the *keyboard* last left the cursor. Cursor moves
  with the keyboard (arrows, Home/End, Ctrl+arrows, Shift+selection,
  Ctrl+A) are followed.
* **Search matches substrings.** The index uses SQLite FTS5's trigram
  tokenizer: a query word matches anywhere inside a word, ignoring case and
  accents (`run` finds "running" and "rerun", `בית` finds "בבית", `cafe`
  finds "Café"). This replaces the design's English-only porter stemmer,
  which cannot find Hebrew words with attached prefixes. Query words
  shorter than 3 characters cannot use the trigram index.
* **Cursor at session start.** When a session starts on text `brain` did
  not see being typed (VS Code replay, or a document after `brain run`
  restarted), the cursor is assumed to be at the end.

where can i see the schema version in brain.db

## Assistant  <sub>2026-11-16T11:56:38.766Z</sub>

The schema version isn't in a table. It's stored in the database file's header as SQLite's built-in `user_version` field, and `brain` sets it to 3 when it creates the database.

**Command line:**
```sh
sqlite3 ~/brain-data/brain.db "PRAGMA user_version;"
```
This prints `3`.

**DB Browser for SQLite** (which you've used): open `brain.db`, then either:
- go to **Execute SQL**, run `PRAGMA user_version;` and the result shows below, or
- go to **Edit Pragmas** and look at the **User Version** field.

Don't edit it there. If you change it, `brain` will refuse the database as a different schema version.

**In the code:** it's the constant `SCHEMA_VERSION` near the top of `src/store.rs`, read and checked in `init_schema` and `open_reader`.

## Assistant  <sub>2026-11-16T12:03:00.892Z</sub>

Fixed. When I replayed your capture log through the new build, typing into the new VS Code file gives **one** session, `testing a changing title`, keyed by `Untitled-1 - ai-logs - Visual Studio Code`.

**The cause:** VS Code names an unsaved file after its first line, so the window title changed on every keystroke (`● t • Untitled-1…`, `● te • Untitled-1…`). Sessions are keyed by window title, so each character started a new session.

**The fix is general, not VS Code-specific**, because email compose windows titled by their subject do the same thing:
- A title change **within 1 s of a keystroke in that same window**, with no shortcut in between, counts as a rename caused by the typing. The session continues under its original title.
- A shortcut such as Ctrl+Tab or Alt+Tab in between means a real tab or window switch, so a new session starts as before.
- When the session closes, the document is also saved under the window's new title. The next session in that window, after the 30 s pause, continues from it.
- One known gap, now in the README: switching tabs **with the mouse** within 1 s of your last keystroke would be mistaken for a rename, since the mouse isn't captured.

**Two more bugs from the same test log:**
- **Tier 2 didn't recognise your VS Code.** Your VS Code's app id is `com.microsoft.VSCode`, and the tier-2 replay only knew the other common ids. It's added now.
- **KRunner's Enter became a newline.** You typed `vsco` + Enter in KRunner, and it was saved as `vsco\n`. Launchers (KRunner, rofi, ulauncher, …) are now single-line fields, so Enter submits.

New tests cover the VS Code rename, a Ctrl+Tab switch that must not count as a rename, and crash recovery in the middle of a rename. All tests pass, including the 25-kill crash test. I added these bugs to "Where the agent failed", since your testing found them and my tests didn't. Pushed as `09cb19d`.

To try it, run `! make` and restart `brain run`. The schema is unchanged, so your current `~/brain-data` works as is.

/// Device-independent key processing: one keymap state shared by all
/// keyboards, as in the compositor.
pub struct KeyProcessor {
    kb: Keyboard,
    repeater: Repeater,
    held: HashMap<u32, HashSet<u16>>, // device id -> held keycodes
}

impl KeyProcessor {
    pub fn new(kb: Keyboard, repeat: RepeatConfig) -> Self {
        Self {
            kb,
            repeater: Repeater::new(repeat),
            held: HashMap::new(),
        }
    }

    /// Replaces the keymap (layout list changed). Held keys are released first.
    pub fn replace_keyboard(&mut self, kb: Keyboard) {
        self.release_all();
        self.kb = kb;
    }

    pub fn set_layout_index(&mut self, index: u32) {
        self.kb.set_layout_index(index);
    }

    pub fn deadline(&self) -> Option<Millis> {
        self.repeater.deadline()
    }

        self.repeater.cancel();
    }

## Assistant  <sub>2026-11-16T12:28:20.875Z</sub>

I found and fixed one real bug in how `brain` handles held keys. What's left is timing inside the apps themselves, which `brain` can't measure. Pushed as `5659f76`.

**The bug (fixed):** after each wakeup, the input loop generated the repeats due "now" *before* reading key releases already waiting in the queue. When the thread woke a little late, a release at time T was read only after repeats scheduled between T and now had been logged. Those were extra characters (or extra Backspaces) the app never saw. The loop now takes the time, reads every queued key event, and only then generates the repeats due by that time.

**The tests:**
1. **Model stress test** (runs with `cargo test`): 300 random scenarios of taps, long holds, holds ending exactly on or 1 ms beside a repeat, overlapping keys, and Shift pressed mid-hold. Wakeups come at random times, early and late, and every emitted key and timestamp must match an independent model of KDE's repeat rule. All pass. A second small test pins down the rule the loop must follow: reading a release late adds a phantom repeat.
2. **Real-app test** (`tests/repeat_e2e.rs`, opt-in): a virtual keyboard holds keys for exact durations in a real Kate window, and Kate's saved file is compared with `brain`.
   - **`brain`'s log now matches KDE's schedule exactly** for every hold, in all three runs.
   - **Kate itself varies.** The same 620 ms hold gave Kate **3, 1 and 2** characters across three runs. On Wayland each app runs its own repeat timer, and Qt apps like Kate use timers that may fire up to 5% early or late. A 600 ms delay can fire anywhere from about 570 to 630 ms, so the app's exact count can't be known from the keyboard.
   - The test therefore checks that the reconstruction is within one character per hold (two for holds over 2 s), with the letters in the same order. Worst case observed: one character.

To run the real-app test yourself (a Kate window types for about 20 s, so hands off the keyboard and mouse):
```
cargo test --release --test repeat_e2e -- --ignored --nocapture
```

The README has a new "Held keys" note under decisions, and the bug is added to "Where the agent failed". Run `! make` to install the fixed build.

Next is `brain query`, unless you want to stress-test something else first.

It passed this time. Your earlier failure was most likely a flaw in my test, not in `brain`. In this run, Kate's held Backspace deleted one character more than `brain` counted, leaving Kate with a single `i` where `brain` has two. Had Kate deleted one more, its last run of `i`s would have vanished completely. Then the "same letters in the same order" check fails, even though every count is within one character. So the Backspace was deleting into a run that's short enough to vanish.

The fix: hold a long key (about 2 s, ~37 characters) right before the Backspace, so Backspace only ever bites into that run and nothing can vanish. I'll commit that together with the Kate cleanup fix.

There are two places:

**1. Unit tests, inside the source files.** Each file in `src/` ends with a test block:
```rust
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    #[test]
    fn some_test() { ... }
}
```
So `capture::keys::tests::repeat_stress_matches_reference_model` lives at the bottom of `src/capture/keys.rs`. The test's name tells you its file: `sessions::tests::…` is in `src/sessions.rs`, `reconstruct::buffer::tests::…` is in `src/reconstruct/buffer.rs`, and so on.

To find one quickly:
```sh
grep -rn "fn repeat_stress_matches_reference_model" src/
```

**2. Integration tests, in `tests/`.** These run the real binary or real apps:

| File | What it tests |
|---|---|

| `tests/vscode_replay.rs` | the VS Code replay against real VS Code (ignored by default) |
| `tests/tier2_e2e.rs` | a VS Code session through ingest to tier 2 (ignored by default) |

**Running them:**
```sh
cargo test                                   # all unit tests + crash_safety
cargo test sessions                          # only tests whose name contains "sessions"

Next is `brain query`. Here's how the time flags and output will work. If any of these choices is wrong, tell me after you see it running; each is easy to change.

**Shared time flags (`search` and `text`)**
- `--from T`, `--to T`, `--at T`. `--at` can't be combined with `--from`/`--to`.
- **T can be any of:**
  - relative: `-90s`, `-15m`, `-2h` (plus `-1d`)
  - `now`
  - full ISO time with a zone: `2026-11-16T14:00:00Z` or `+02:00`
  - **local** time: `2026-11-16 14:00`, `2026-11-16T14:00:30`, a date alone (local midnight), or a time alone (`14:00`, meaning today)
- **Windows:**
  - `--at T` means the 10 minutes ending at T, for both commands.
  - `--from` alone runs from T to now.
  - `--to` alone: for `text`, the 10 minutes ending at T (as your design says); for `search`, everything up to T.
  - No flags: `text` shows the last 10 minutes; `search` covers all time.
- **Output:** times stay in UTC `…Z`, the format of the assignment's example. The echoed window is included, so you can see how your local input was read.

**`search`**
- Every word must appear in the same session, as a substring, ignoring case.
- Open sessions are included, so it finds what you're typing right now; those have `ended_at: null`.
- Newest first, with a snippet around the first match.

**`text`**
- The raw stream of what was typed, read from the log:
  - characters as typed
  - Enter as a newline, Tab as a tab
  - other keys and shortcuts as `<Backspace>`, `<Left>`, `<Ctrl+V>`
  - pasted text inline
- No editing is applied; that's the session text's job.

**`--app`** matches part of the app id, ignoring case, so `--app chrome` finds `google-chrome`.

//! Timestamps: everything internal is milliseconds since the Unix epoch (UTC).
//!
//! On disk and in JSON output, timestamps are RFC 3339 in UTC with millisecond
//! precision (`2026-11-08T14:03:22.118Z`). Fixed width and UTC means the
//! strings sort lexicographically in time order, which the SQLite schema
//! relies on.

use anyhow::{Result, bail};
use chrono::{DateTime, Local, NaiveDateTime, TimeZone, Utc};
use std::time::{SystemTime, UNIX_EPOCH};

/// Milliseconds since the Unix epoch, UTC.
pub type Millis = i64;

pub fn now_ms() -> Millis {
    system_time_ms(SystemTime::now())
}

pub fn system_time_ms(t: SystemTime) -> Millis {
    match t.duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH) {
        Ok(d) => d.as_millis() as Millis,
        Err(e) => -(e.duration().as_millis() as Millis),
    }
}

/// Formats as `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.mmmZ`.
pub fn format_ms(ms: Millis) -> String {
    match Utc.timestamp_millis_opt(ms).single() {
        Some(dt) => dt.format("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%.3fZ").to_string(),
        // Out of chrono's range; cannot happen for real clock readings.
        None => "1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z".to_string(),
    }
}

/// Parses an RFC 3339 timestamp (any offset), as written in the log.
pub fn parse_rfc3339_ms(s: &str) -> Result<Millis> {
    Ok(DateTime::parse_from_rfc3339(s)?.timestamp_millis())
}

/// Parses a user-supplied time for `--at`, `--from` and `--to`.
///
/// Accepted forms:
/// * RFC 3339 with an offset: `2026-11-08T14:03:22Z`, `2026-11-08T16:03:22+02:00`
/// * local time without an offset: `2026-11-08T14:03`, `2026-11-08 14:03:22`
/// * a local date: `2026-11-08` (midnight local time)
pub fn parse_user_time(s: &str) -> Result<Millis> {
    let s = s.trim();
    if let Ok(dt) = DateTime::parse_from_rfc3339(s) {
        return Ok(dt.timestamp_millis());
    }
    const LOCAL_FORMATS: &[&str] = &[
        "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%.f",
        "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%.f",
        "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M",
        "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M",
    ];
    for fmt in LOCAL_FORMATS {
        if let Ok(naive) = NaiveDateTime::parse_from_str(s, fmt) {
            return local_to_ms(naive, s);
        }
    }
    if let Ok(date) = chrono::NaiveDate::parse_from_str(s, "%Y-%m-%d") {
        let naive = date.and_hms_opt(0, 0, 0).expect("midnight is valid");
        return local_to_ms(naive, s);
    }
    bail!(
        "invalid time {s:?}: expected RFC 3339 (2026-11-08T14:03:22Z) or local \
         'YYYY-MM-DD[ HH:MM[:SS]]'"
    )
}

fn local_to_ms(naive: NaiveDateTime, original: &str) -> Result<Millis> {
    match Local.from_local_datetime(&naive) {
        chrono::LocalResult::Single(dt) => Ok(dt.timestamp_millis()),
        // DST fold: the earlier instant is the conventional choice.
        chrono::LocalResult::Ambiguous(earlier, _) => Ok(earlier.timestamp_millis()),
        chrono::LocalResult::None => {
            bail!("time {original:?} does not exist in the local time zone (DST gap)")
        }
    }

/// The app value used for global (all-app) checkpoints.
pub const GLOBAL_CHECKPOINT_APP: &str = "*";

/// Opens the database for the writer (`brain run`), creating it if new.
pub fn open_writer(path: &Path) -> Result<Connection> {
    let conn =
        Connection::open(path).with_context(|| format!("opening database {}", path.display()))?;
pub fn set_ingest_offset(conn: &Connection, offset: u64) -> Result<()> {
    conn.execute(
        "UPDATE ingest_state SET log_offset = ?1 WHERE id = 1",
        [offset as i64],
    )?;
    Ok(())
}

pub fn insert_checkpoint(conn: &Connection, app: &str, ts: &str, offset: u64) -> Result<()> {
    conn.prepare_cached(
        "INSERT OR IGNORE INTO log_checkpoints (app, ts, byte_offset) VALUES (?1, ?2, ?3)",
    )?
    .execute(rusqlite::params![app, ts, offset as i64])?;
    Ok(())
}

/// Latest checkpoint timestamp per app, used to resume checkpoint spacing after a restart.
pub fn latest_checkpoints(conn: &Connection) -> Result<Vec<(String, String)>> {
    let mut stmt = conn.prepare("SELECT app, MAX(ts) FROM log_checkpoints GROUP BY app")?;
    let rows = stmt
        .query_map([], |r| Ok((r.get::<_, String>(0)?, r.get::<_, String>(1)?)))?
        .collect::<rusqlite::Result<Vec<_>>>()?;
    Ok(rows)
}

/// Byte offset of the latest global checkpoint at or before `ts`, or 0.
pub fn seek_offset_before(conn: &Connection, ts: &str) -> Result<u64> {
    let off: Option<i64> = conn
        .query_row(
            "SELECT byte_offset FROM log_checkpoints WHERE app = ?1 AND ts <= ?2
             ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 1",
            rusqlite::params![GLOBAL_CHECKPOINT_APP, ts],
            |r| r.get(0),
        )
        .optional()?;
    Ok(off.unwrap_or(0) as u64)
}

Explain how are the global bookmarks entries are used, by design and in code, how is the timestamp alone good enough

## Assistant  <sub>2026-11-16T15:15:45.698Z</sub>

## What a bookmark is

Each row in `log_checkpoints` is `(ts, byte_offset)`: "the event at byte `byte_offset` of `events.jsonl` has timestamp `ts`". There is at most one per 5 s of log time.

## Writing them (`src/ingest.rs`, `try_step`)

While ingest reads each new line, inside the same transaction as everything else:

```rust
if checkpoint_due(staged.or(self.last_checkpoint), event.ts) {   // ≥ 5 s since the last one
    store::insert_checkpoint(&tx, &format_ms(event.ts), line.offset)?;
    staged = Some(event.ts);
}
```

- The first event after a 5 s gap becomes a bookmark, pointing at the start of its own line.
- "5 s since" is measured as an absolute difference, so a clock that jumps *backwards* also creates a new bookmark right away.
- They're committed together with the log position, so a crash can't leave a bookmark pointing past what was ingested, or skip one. The crash test checks they equal a clean rebuild.

## Reading them (`src/query.rs`, `text`)

```rust
let start = store::seek_offset_before(&conn, &format_ms(from))?;   // latest bookmark with ts ≤ from
let mut reader = LogReader::open(&dir.log_path(), start)?;
while let Some(line) = reader.next_line()? {
    if ev.ts > to + 60 s { break; }                                // stop a bit past the window
    if ev.ts < from || ev.ts > to || !app matches { continue; }    // filter while reading
    render the key / paste
}
```

So `text` jumps to just before the window, reads forward, keeps only that app's events inside the window, and stops shortly after the window ends.

## Why a timestamp alone is enough, and why no app is needed

- **The log is in time order.** One writer appends each event the moment it happens, stamped with that moment. So every line before a bookmark has an earlier timestamp. If a bookmark's `ts ≤ from`, nothing in the window can sit before it, and starting there misses nothing.
- **The cost is bounded.** The jump lands at most 5 s of log before `from`, and reading stops 60 s of log after `to`. A 10-minute `--at` reads about 10–11 minutes of log, not the whole file.
- **Per-app bookmarks couldn't save any work.** The log interleaves all apps, so the lines between `from` and `to` have to be read anyway to find one app's events. A per-app bookmark could only move the starting point by up to 5 s. That's why I dropped them.

## Where "time order" isn't guaranteed

The timestamps come from the wall clock, which can be stepped backwards: an NTP correction, or someone changing the system time. Say the clock jumps back 2 minutes at 10:05. Lines written after the jump carry 10:03…, but sit *after* lines that carry 10:03–10:05.

1. **Start point.** For `--from 10:04`, "latest bookmark with ts ≤ 10:04" can pick a bookmark written *after* the jump. Reading starts past the pre-jump lines stamped 10:04–10:05 and misses them.
2. **Stop point.** The "60 s past the window" stop assumes the clock doesn't jump back by more than 60 s later on. If it does, events in the window that come after that jump are missed.

That's rare on a desktop, but both cases are real.

**This can be made exact, still with timestamps alone.** The bookmarks already guarantee one thing even when the clock jumps: every line is within 5 s of the last bookmark before it, because a bigger difference in either direction creates a new bookmark. So:
- **Start** at the *earliest* bookmark, by position in the file, with `ts > from − 5 s`. Every line with `ts ≥ from` has such a bookmark at or before it.
- **Stop** at the bookmark that follows the *last* one, by position, with `ts < to + 5 s`. No later line can be inside the window. If no bookmark follows, read to the end of the file, which also covers the lines written in the last second that ingest hasn't bookmarked yet.

With an ordinary clock, this reads the same amount as now. With a jumping clock, it reads more, but misses nothing, and the 60 s guess goes away.

Should I implement it? It's two small SQL queries plus a test where the clock jumps backwards in the log.

utime and stime are the\n    // 14th and 15th fields overall.\n    let rest = &stat[stat.rfind(')').unwrap() + 2..];\n    let f: Vec<&str> = rest.split_whitespace().collect();\n    f[11].parse::<u64>().unwrap() + f[12].parse::<u64>().unwrap()\n}\n\n/// Peak resident set size (VmHWM) of `pid`, in kB.\nfn peak_rss_kb(pid: u32) -> u64 {\n    let status = std::fs::read_to_string(format!(\"/proc/{pid}/status\")).unwrap();\n    status\n        .lines()\n        .find_map(|l| l.strip_prefix(\"VmHWM:\"))\n        .and_then(|v| v.trim().trim_end_matches(\"kB\").trim().parse().ok())\n        .unwrap()\n}\n\n#[test]\nfn cpu_and_memory_stay_within_budget_while_typing() {\n    let tmp = tempfile::tempdir().unwrap();\n    let dir = tmp.path().join(\"data\");\n    let mut run = Command::new(env!(\"CARGO_BIN_EXE_brain\"))\n        .args([\"run\", \"--synthetic\", &KEYS_PER_SECOND.to_string(), \"--data-dir\"])\n        .arg(&dir)\n        .stdout(Stdio::null())\n        .stderr(Stdio::null())\n        .spawn()\n        .unwrap();\n    let pid = run.id();\n    std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(2)); // past startup\n\n    // SAFETY: sysconf is always safe to call.\n    let hz = unsafe { libc::sysconf(libc::_SC_CLK_TCK) } as f64;\n    let start_ticks = cpu_ticks(pid);\n    let start = Instant::now();\n    let mut queries = 0;\n    while start.elapsed() < MEASURE {\n        std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(3));\n        let out = Command::new(env!(\"CARGO_BIN_EXE_brain\"))\n            .args([\"query\", \"search\", \"migration\", \"--data-dir\"])\n            .arg(&dir)\n            .output()\n            .unwrap();\n        assert!(out.status.success());\n        queries += 1;\n    }\n    let elapsed = start.elapsed().as_secs_f64();\n    let cpu = (cpu_ticks(pid) - start_ticks) as f64 / hz / elapsed * 100.0;\n    let rss = peak_rss_kb(pid);\n    // SAFETY: SIGTERM to our own child.\n    unsafe { libc::kill(pid as i32, libc::SIGTERM) };\n    assert!(run.wait().unwrap().success());\n\n    // The typing really went through the whole pipeline.\n    let log = std::fs::read_to_string(dir.join(\"events.jsonl\")).unwrap();\n    let keys = log.lines().filter(|l| l.contains(\"\\\"type\\\":\\\"key\\\"\")).count();\n    eprintln!(\n        \"{keys} keys in {elapsed:.0}s with {queries} queries: \\\n         CPU {cpu:.3}% (budget {MAX_CPU_PERCENT}%), peak RSS {} kB (budget {MAX_RSS_KB} kB)\",\n        rss\n    );\n    assert!(keys as f64 > KEYS_PER_SECOND as f64 * elapsed * 0.8, \"only {keys} keys\");\n    assert!(cpu <= MAX_CPU_PERCENT, \"CPU {cpu:.3}% over budget\");\n    assert!(rss <= MAX_RSS_KB, \"peak RSS {rss} kB over budget\");\n}\n"
}

69	## 2. Research: collecting keystrokes and application data
70	
71	### 2.1 The constraint that shapes everything: Wayland
72	
73	On X11, any client can read global input (XRecord, XInput2 raw events) and the
74	active window (`_NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW`). Wayland removed both on purpose. Clients
75	only receive input while they have focus, and there is no standard protocol
76	for asking "which window is active". Global capture therefore needs one of:
77	kernel-level input access, cooperation from the compositor, or cooperation from
78	each application. Every approach below falls into one of those three groups.
79	
80	### 2.2 Keystrokes: approaches compared
81	
82	| # | Approach | Works on KDE Wayland? | What it sees | Permissions | Latency / CPU | Text fidelity | Robustness | Invasiveness / risk |

763	## 7. Resource budget
764	
765	Targets: no input lag, ≤ 1% average CPU while typing, ≤ 32 MB memory.
766	
767	**No input lag by construction.** brain is a passive evdev reader, not on the
768	delivery path (2.2). Nothing it does, including stalling completely, can delay
769	a keystroke reaching the compositor.
770	
771	**CPU.**
772	
773	- No async runtime. The capture thread is one `epoll` loop over evdev fds, the
774	  inotify fd, the repeat `timerfd` and the fsync `timerfd`. It sleeps in
775	  `epoll_wait` between events: no polling, no busy timers.
776	- Per keystroke: one `read()` of a few `input_event`s, an xkbcommon state
777	  update and keysym lookup (sub-µs), JSON formatting into a reused buffer, and
778	  one `write()` (~1–5 µs into the page cache). At a fast ~10 keystrokes/s that
779	  is well under 100 µs of CPU per second: < 0.01% of a core. Holding a key
780	  (25 Hz repeat) is within the same order.
781	- `fdatasync` at most once per second while typing.
782	- Ingest wakes per durable-offset bump (≤ 1/s) and does one small SQLite
783	  transaction. FTS work per session is proportional to the session's text
784	  (bytes to kB).
785	- D-Bus: zbus's blocking API (it runs a small internal executor thread). There
786	  is traffic only on focus/caption changes.
787	- The KWin script is event-driven inside KWin and does no work between window
788	  events.
789	
790	**Memory.**
791	
792	- No tokio. Three threads plus zbus's internal one, with small stacks.
793	- SQLite `cache_size` ~2 MB, no mmap, one connection on the writer side.
794	- Context buffers capped and evicted (4.6). The repeat and sessionizer state
795	  is O(open contexts).
796	- Expected steady-state RSS: low single-digit MB for capture, plus a few MB
797	  for SQLite and zbus. Comfortably under 32 MB, and asserted in tests (below).
798	
799	**How it is verified.**
800	
801	- A perf harness generates keystrokes through a virtual keyboard
802	  (`evemu-play` or a tiny uinput program; only the *generator* needs uinput
803	  access, brain runs unprivileged) at 10 keys/s with realistic Backspace and
804	  focus changes for 10 minutes. It samples brain's `utime+stime` from
805	  `/proc/<pid>/stat` and `VmRSS`/`VmHWM` from `/proc/<pid>/status`, and fails
806	  if average CPU > 1% or peak RSS > 32 MB.
807	- Latency: the same harness compares evdev timestamps with logged timestamps
808	  (they must be identical, because the kernel stamp is propagated), and
809	  measures write-to-ingest delay.
810	- `perf stat` / `strace -c` spot checks to confirm one `write()` per event and
811	  no stray wake-ups while idle.

819	
820	- **Data at rest.** `brain-data/` is created 0700 and its files 0600.

## Assistant  <sub>2026-11-16T21:40:34.792Z</sub>

This is a real bug in `brain`. Kate got it right ("beta" went to window B), but `brain` filed "beta" under window A's session.

**Cause:** the rename rule I added for VS Code's new-file titles. The test typed " world" in Kate A, then opened Kate B, which took focus within 1 s. Same app, a different title, under 1 s after a keystroke, and no shortcut in between, so `brain` decided A had been renamed to B. The rule can't tell a title change *inside the same window* from *a different window being activated*.

**Fix:** KWin knows the difference. It sends `windowActivated` when a different window gets focus, and `captionChanged` when the same window's title changes. The KWin script will pass that on, and focus events in the log will carry `"renamed": true` for title changes. Then:
- A **window activation** ends any possible rename. So opening or switching to another window, by keyboard or **by mouse**, is never mistaken for one. That also fixes part of the mouse gap I'd documented.
- Only a **title change of the window that was typed in**, within 1 s and with no shortcut in between, keeps the session.

Here's the KWin script and the focus path:

**Tool call: `Bash`**

```

  "command": "cat src/capture/kwin_focus.js; grep -n 'fn activated' -B3 -A25 src/capture/desktop.rs; grep -n 'pub fn set_focus' -A30 src/capture/recorder.rs; grep -rn 'set_focus(' src | grep -v 'fn set_focus'; grep -rn 'EventKind::Focus' src tests | cut -c1-120",
  "description": "Read KWin script, D-Bus handler, recorder focus and uses"
}

// Generated by `brain run`; loaded into KWin over D-Bus and unloaded on exit.
//
// Wayland gives ordinary clients no way to ask "which window is focused?", so
// this script runs inside the compositor and pushes every activation and
// active-window title change to brain's D-Bus service.
const SERVICE = "@SERVICE@";
const PATH = "@PATH@";
const IFACE = "@IFACE@";

function report(w) {
    if (w) {
        callDBus(SERVICE, PATH, IFACE, "Activated",
                 String(w.desktopFileName || ""), String(w.resourceClass || ""), String(w.caption || ""));
    } else {
        callDBus(SERVICE, PATH, IFACE, "Activated", "", "", "");
    }
}

function watch(w) {
    // Title changes mark a new context in the same app: a browser tab switch,
    // another file in the editor, a new command in the terminal title.
    w.captionChanged.connect(function () {
        if (workspace.activeWindow === w) {
            report(w);
        }
    });
}

workspace.windowList().forEach(watch);
workspace.windowAdded.connect(watch);
workspace.windowActivated.connect(report);

## Assistant  <sub>2026-11-16T21:46:25.323Z</sub>

Everything is done and pushed (`ee3f508`), and every test suite passes on the finished build, including both Kate tests. Your real-keyboard run found one more real bug in `brain`, which is now fixed.

**The bug:** text typed in a second Kate window was filed under the first window's session. The rule that keeps VS Code's new-file session together (a title change shortly after typing counts as a rename) also fired when another Kate window opened less than a second after typing.

**The fix:** KWin knows whether focus moved to a different window or the same window's title changed, and now passes that on. Focus events in the log carry `"renamed": true` for title changes. Only a title change of the window you typed in can count as a rename. Activating any other window, including by mouse click, never does. A regression test reproduces the exact Kate sequence.

**Final results:**

## Assistant  <sub>2026-11-16T22:02:10.047Z</sub>

Two changes:
1. **Local times in all `query` output:** result times and the echoed window become RFC 3339 with your offset, e.g. `2026-11-16T16:51:14.684+02:00` instead of `…14:51:14.684Z`. The log and database keep storing UTC.
2. **`text` reports the real app id.** `--app` still accepts part of a name, but the output's `app` is the full id, e.g. `--app kate` gives `"app": "org.kde.kate"`. How the name gets resolved:
   - The candidates are the app ids in the database plus those seen in the requested window.
   - If one matches the input exactly (ignoring case), that one wins.
   - Otherwise, if exactly one id contains it, that's the app.
   - If several contain it, it's an error listing them, so text from different apps never gets mixed.
   - If none do, it's an error too, listing the known apps. An app that exists but had no typing in the window still returns empty text.

/// The raw typed stream of the apps matching `app`, over the window: every
/// key as captured, with no editing applied (see [`render_key`]), and pasted
/// text inline.
pub fn text(dir: &DataDir, app: &str, flags: &TimeFlags, now: Millis) -> Result<TextOutput> {
    let w = resolve(flags, Command::Text, now)?;
    let (from, to) = (w.from.unwrap_or(Millis::MIN), w.to.unwrap_or(now));
    let conn = store::open_reader(&dir.db_path())?;
    let start = store::seek_offset_before(&conn, &timefmt::format_ms(from))?;
    drop(conn);
    let needle = app.to_lowercase();
    let mut out = String::new();
    if dir.log_path().exists() {
        let mut reader = LogReader::open(&dir.log_path(), start)?;
        while let Some(line) = reader.next_line()? {
            let Some(ev) = line.event else { continue };
            if ev.ts > to.saturating_add(CLOCK_SLACK_MS) {
                break;
            }
            if ev.ts < from || ev.ts > to || !ev.app.to_lowercase().contains(&needle) {
                continue;
            }
            match ev.kind {
                EventKind::Key { key, mods, .. } => render_key(&key, &mods, &mut out),
                EventKind::Paste {
                    text: Some(text), ..
                } => out.push_str(&text),
                _ => {}
            }
        }
    }
    Ok(TextOutput {
        app: app.to_string(),
        at: fmt_opt(w.at),
        from: fmt_opt(w.from),
        to: fmt_opt(w.to),
        text: out,
    })
}

Both changes are in, tested and pushed (`c9f9bb9`).

**1. Local times in query output.** Every time in `search` results (`started_at`, `ended_at`) and the echoed window in both commands (`from`, `to`, `at`) is now in your local zone, with the offset:
```
"started_at": "2026-11-17T00:04:38.044+02:00"
```
That's still standard RFC 3339, so it stays unambiguous. The log and the database keep storing UTC.

**2. `text` reports the full app id.**
```
$ brain query text --app kons --from -3s
{ "app": "org.kde.konsole", ... }
```
- The candidates are the apps that have sessions, plus any app with keys or pastes in the requested window. Events that aren't typing, like the `start` event, don't count.
- An exact match wins, ignoring case. So `--app code` means `code` even though `com.microsoft.VSCode` also contains "code".
- Otherwise the one id that contains your text wins.
- **If several match, it's an error** listing them, so `text` never mixes two apps into one stream:
  `brain: error: "o" matches several apps: org.kde.konsole, synthetic; be more specific`
- **If none match, it's also an error**, listing the known apps. Before, it quietly returned empty text.
- A known app that had no typing in the window still returns empty text, with its full id.
- `search --app` is unchanged: it keeps every matching app, and each result already shows its full id.

**Tests:** new unit tests for the name resolution (exact over partial, several matches, none) and for local-time formatting. The CLI tests now check local times, full ids, and both error cases. Everything passes: 121 unit tests, crash safety, `query_cli`, `perf_budget`. The README and PLAN.md describe the new behavior.

No database change this time, so `! make` is all you need to use it.

**Notes on the rows that were close calls:**

- **evdev (A) vs libinput (B).** Both read the same device nodes. libinput's
  value is pointer acceleration, touchpad gestures and tablet handling, none of
  which we need. For keys it adds nothing over `struct input_event`. Reading
  evdev directly keeps the dependency set and the memory footprint small, and
  gives full control over hotplug and resync.
- **Why not grab (D).** A passive reader is *not on the input path*: the kernel
  delivers each event to every open evdev client independently. If brain
  stalls, the user notices nothing. A grab-and-forward proxy makes every
  keystroke wait on brain, needs root for `/dev/uinput`, and its failure mode
  (frozen keyboard) is the worst one possible. It only makes sense for tools
  that *modify* input (remappers); we only observe.
- **AT-SPI (F)** is the only system-wide source that sees real text rather than
  keys, and it is tempting for exactly that reason. In practice, coverage
  decides: our three target app classes (Chrome/Electron, VS Code, terminals)
  are the weak spots. It needs browser flags and a11y forced on, and terminal
  emulators expose little of their contents. It stays a future enhancement, as
  a *second source* that could correct key-based reconstruction for GTK/Qt
  apps. It would not replace evdev.
- **Compositor hook (H)** has the best key-level fidelity, but a plugin
  compiled against one KWin version and loaded into the user's compositor is a
  bad trade for a home-assignment tool: an ABI mismatch or a bug takes down the
  desktop. We take the one thing we need from the compositor (focus) through
  its *supported* scripting interface, and copy its keymap and repeat settings
  instead of hooking it.

## Supported OS

Ubuntu (tested on 26.04) with **KDE Plasma 6 on Wayland** (KWin). Key capture
works on any Linux. Focus tracking needs KWin (Wayland or X11). On other
desktops, keys are recorded under the app `unknown`.

## Build

```sh
# Rust toolchain (https://rustup.rs), then:
cargo build --release
# binary: target/release/brain

# or build and install to /usr/bin/brain (asks for sudo for the copy only):
make
```

SQLite is bundled. libxkbcommon is loaded from the runtime library
`libxkbcommon.so.0` that every Wayland desktop ships, so no `-dev`
packages are needed.

## Permissions

`brain` reads keyboards directly from `/dev/input/event*` (read-only,
never grabbed, so it cannot add input lag). Your user must be in the `input`
group:

```sh
sudo usermod -aG input "$USER"   # then log out and back in
```

Note that the `input` group can read every input device. That is the price of
display-server-independent capture (see PLAN.md for the alternatives).

## Run

```sh
target/release/brain run --data-dir ~/brain-data
```

`run` stops cleanly on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. A `kill -9` is also safe. The next
start repairs a torn last line, if there is one, and resumes ingest exactly
where it stopped.

### As a service

`brain` can run as a **systemd user service**: it starts with your Plasma
session, restarts if it crashes, stops at logout, and runs as you (no
root; it needs your desktop session for focus tracking):

```sh
make install-service          # installs /usr/bin/brain + the unit, enables it
journalctl --user -u brain -f # its messages
systemctl --user stop brain   # pause capture
make uninstall-service        # remove it
```

The service uses `~/brain-data`. Stop it before running `brain run` by hand
on the same directory (only one `brain run` per data directory).

Add `--vscode-replay` to reconstruct VS Code sessions in a sandboxed,
invisible copy of VS Code (tier 2, below). It is off by default.

Data directory (mode 0700):

| File           | What                                                   |
|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| `events.jsonl` | append-only capture log, the ground truth              |
| `brain.db`     | SQLite (WAL) index derived from the log                |
| `run.lock`     | held by the running `brain run` (one per data dir)     |
| `kwin/`        | generated KWin focus-tracking script                   |
| `vscode/`      | VS Code replay sandbox and file snapshots (tier 2 only) |

Example log lines:

```json
{"ts":"2026-11-15T17:20:01.112Z","app":"org.kde.konsole","type":"focus","window":"~ : bash — Konsole"}
{"ts":"2026-11-15T17:20:02.348Z","app":"org.kde.konsole","type":"key","key":"H","mods":["shift"],"window":"~ : bash — Konsole"}
```

# CLAUDE.md — instructions for coding agents working on `brain`

`brain` is a Rust CLI for the Endpoint "Shadow Assistant" home assignment
(`Endpoint Home Assignment.pdf`, not committed). One binary, two commands:
`brain run` captures keystrokes + focus and stores them; `brain query`
(`search`, `text`) answers questions while `run` keeps going.

Design doc (source of truth for architecture):
https://claude.ai/artifact/UTxCHmXHeSBaQASSNNiSP9 — `PLAN.md` is the in-repo
research/architecture write-up and must stay consistent with the code.

## Target platform

Ubuntu, **KDE Plasma 6 on Wayland** (KWin). Not GNOME. Keys come from evdev
(`/dev/input/event*`, user in the `input` group), resolved with libxkbcommon
(`libxkbcommon.so.0`, linked by file name, so no `-dev` package is needed).
Focus comes from a KWin script calling back over D-Bus. `/dev/uinput` is
root-only on the dev machine: tests must not depend on it. Use
`brain run --synthetic RATE` (hidden flag) to drive the real pipeline without
hardware.

## Hard requirements (from the assignment) — never regress these

- Capture is invisible: no input lag (we never grab devices), **≤ 1 % average
  CPU while typing, ≤ 32 MB RSS**, keeps working after sleep/wake.
- `kill -9` of `run` at any moment + restart ⇒ no corruption
  (`tests/crash_safety.rs` must stay green).
- `query` works while `run` writes and always sees a consistent state.
- Both commands take `--data-dir` (default `./brain-data`) and exit non-zero
  with a message on stderr on error. Query output is JSON on stdout.

## Decisions already made by the owner — do not re-litigate

- `brain query text` returns the **raw decoded keystroke stream** (no
  backspace/cursor editing applied) over a window: default last 10 min,
  `--at T` = 10-min window ending at T, or `--from/--to`.
- Sessions: keyed by (app, window); close after 30 s idle in that context or
  on Enter in single-line contexts; focus loss alone never closes a session.
- Reconstruction tiers: 0 = generic buffer replay, 1 = per-app rules,
  2 = VS Code real-app replay, **opt-in** via `brain run --vscode-replay`,
  falling back to tier 0. Sessions, reconstruction and indexing are built
  before `brain query` (owner's call, changing the original stage order).
- Search is substring matching (FTS5 trigram, case- and accent-insensitive),
  not the design's porter stemming: `run` must find "rerun", `בית` "בבית".
- Sessions and their text must stay a pure function of the log: the crash
  test compares the live index with a fresh rebuild.
- Work proceeds in 4 stages (capture, query, reconstruction, E2E tests).
  After each stage: build, run, test it yourself, report, then **stop and
  wait for explicit approval** before the next stage.

## Sessions and reconstruction

Ingest (inside `brain run`, about once a second) turns the log into
**writing sessions**, stored in the `sessions` table with an FTS5 index.

* A session is one `(app, window title)`. Markers that change while you
  type are removed from the title first: an editor's unsaved-file dot or
  `*`, and the spinner glyphs terminal programs animate (`◐ ◑ ⠹ ✳`).
  When the title changes *because of the typing* (VS Code names a new file
  after its first line, a mail window after its subject), the session
  continues: a change of the *same* window's title (KWin tells a title
  change from a window activation) within 1 s of a keystroke in it, with no
  shortcut in between, is treated as a rename. It closes after **30 s without
  typing in that window**, or right away when a single-line field is
  submitted (Enter at a shell prompt, in a chat box or a browser's address
  bar), cancelled (Ctrl+C at a prompt), or left for another field of the
  same window (Tab, Ctrl+L in a browser). Switching to another app and back
  within 30 s continues the same session. Stopping or restarting `brain run`
  closes all sessions.
* While a session is open, its text so far is already in the index, so a
  search finds what you are typing right now.
* **Tier 0**: keys are replayed into a virtual text field with a cursor,
  selection, word-wise movement and deletion, and undo/redo. Only keyboard
  cursor movement is followed (see "Decisions and edge cases").
* **Tier 1**: a small table of app classes decides what keys mean. In
  terminals: readline shortcuts (Ctrl+A/E/U/K/W) and Up/Down history recall
  from the commands `brain` saw you run. In browsers: Tab and Ctrl+L/K/T/W
  move to another field. Enter submits single-line fields and inserts a
  newline elsewhere. Editors and unknown apps keep their document across
  sessions. Single-line fields start empty each time.
* **Tier 2** (`--vscode-replay`): when a VS Code session closes, its
  keystrokes are replayed into a headless VS Code with your settings, in a
  network-less sandbox with capped CPU and memory. The session text then
  comes from VS Code itself (auto-indent, bracket pairs, your keybindings).
  The session stores the changed lines. If replay is impossible or fails,
  the tier 0/1 text stays.

Inspect the result:

sqlite3 ~/brain-data/brain.db \
  "SELECT id, app, started_at, ended_at, status, end_reason, tier_used, reconstructed_text FROM sessions"
```

**Queries**
* **`query text` is the raw stream, `search` the edited text.** As the
  owner decided, `text` returns exactly what was typed (with `<Backspace>`
  and other keys visible) rather than reconstructed text; reconstructed,
  edit-aware text is what `search` matches and returns.
* **Search matches substrings.** The index uses SQLite FTS5's trigram
  tokenizer: a query word matches anywhere inside a word, ignoring case and
  accents (`run` finds "running" and "rerun", `בית` finds "בבית", `cafe`
  finds "Café"). This replaces the design's English-only porter stemmer,
  which cannot find Hebrew words with attached prefixes. Query words
  shorter than 3 characters cannot use the trigram index and are matched
  with a slower scan.
* **Times in, times out are local.** `--from`, `--to` and `--at` accept
  relative times (`-2h`), local dates and times, and RFC 3339; output times
  are local with their offset. The log and the database store UTC.
* **`--app` takes part of the id.** `search` keeps every matching app;
  `text` must resolve to exactly one app and reports its full id, so two
  apps' keystrokes are never mixed into one stream.
* **`query text` assumes the log is in time order.** It starts reading at
  the last checkpoint before its window and stops 60 s of log after it. If
  the system clock is stepped backwards while capturing (an NTP correction,
  a manual change), keys typed after the step whose times fall in a queried
  window can be missed. PLAN.md (section 10) describes an exact bound.

**Running**

## User  <sub>2026-11-17T09:33:49.020Z</sub>

explain how does query text work today

## Assistant  <sub>2026-11-17T09:34:11.260Z</sub>

`brain query text` reads the raw keystrokes straight from the log, not from the sessions table, and prints one app's stream for a time window. Here are the steps, following `query::text` in `src/query.rs`:

**1. Parse the CLI** (`src/main.rs`)
- `--app A` is required. `--at`, `--from` and `--to` are optional. `--at` can't be combined with the other two, which clap enforces.
- It checks that the data folder and `brain.db` exist, and stops with an error if not.
- It takes "now" once, so every relative time in the command uses the same reference.

**2. Work out the window** (`resolve`)
- Each time flag is parsed: relative (`-2h`), local (`14:00`, `2026-11-17 09:00`), or RFC 3339.
- Then:

| Flags | Window |
|---|---|
| none | the last 10 minutes |
| `--at T` | T − 10 min … T |
| `--from A` | A … now |
| `--to B` | B − 10 min … B |
| `--from A --to B` | A … B |

- If the window starts after it ends, that's an error.

**3. Read two things from the database**, read-only:
- **Where to start in the log:** the byte position of the latest bookmark at or before the window's start (`log_checkpoints`). Bookmarks are at most 5 s apart, so reading starts at most 5 s before the window.
- **The known apps:** every distinct app id in `sessions`. These are candidates for resolving `--app`.

**4. Read the log forward** from that byte (`LogReader`, which returns only complete lines, never one still being written):
- Lines that don't parse are skipped.
- **It stops** at the first event more than 60 s past the window's end. That margin allows for small clock wobbles.
- **It keeps** only events that are inside the window, are typing (a key or a paste), and whose app id contains the `--app` text, ignoring case.
- Each kept event is held in memory together with its app id, and each such app is added to the candidate list.
- Focus, lock and sleep events are ignored.

**5. Resolve `--app` to one app** (`resolve_app`), among the apps with sessions plus those that typed in the window:
- An exact match wins, ignoring case: `code` is `code`, even though `com.microsoft.VSCode` also contains it.
- Otherwise, the one id that contains the text.
- **Several matches are an error** listing them, so two apps' streams are never mixed. **No match is an error** too: it lists the known apps, or says nothing has been typed yet.

**6. Render that app's events in log order** (`render_key`), with no editing applied:

| Event | Output |
|---|---|
| a typed character (Shift/AltGr already applied: `H`, `ש`, `€`) | the character |
| Enter / Tab | a newline / a tab |
| any other key | `<Backspace>`, `<Left>`, `<Delete>`, … |
| a shortcut | `<Ctrl+V>`, `<Ctrl+Shift+V>`, `<Alt+Tab>` |
| a paste | the pasted text, inline |

Held-key repeats are included, because the app received them. So a held Backspace shows as several `<Backspace>`.

**7. Print the JSON**, with times in local time:
```json
{
  "app": "org.kde.konsole",
  "at": null,
  "from": "2026-11-17T10:00:00.000+02:00",
  "to": "2026-11-17T10:10:00.000+02:00",
  "text": "git staus<Backspace><Backspace>tus\n"
}
```
`app` is the full id, and `from`/`to`/`at` echo the window that was actually used.

**While `brain run` is writing:** the bookmark comes from a consistent database snapshot. The log reader never returns a half-written line. Lines appended after the read started may or may not be included, which is fine either way. Events from the last second, not yet ingested, are still read because they're in the log.

**Cost:** about the window's length plus at most 5 s of log is read, so a 10-minute query reads about 10 minutes of log whatever its total size. Only that app's matching events are held in memory.

**Limitations:**
- If the system clock is stepped backwards while capturing, keys typed after that point can be missed. That's the "time order" assumption we discussed; it's documented.
- An app that never had a session and typed nothing in the window can't be resolved. Asking for it is an error, though nothing would be printed for it anyway.

## Assistant  <sub>2026-11-17T09:41:11.123Z</sub>

To confirm what I'm changing: until now `query text` returned the raw stream, as you'd originally decided. From now on it returns **reconstructed** text, built with the same session and reconstruction code `search` uses. No second implementation.

**What `text` will return:** the app's text **as it stood at the end of the window**.
- **Sessions that ended inside the window:** their stored final text, as already in the database (tier 2 included).
- **Sessions still running at the end of the window**, e.g. `--at 10:05` when you kept typing until 10:20: the session is replayed from its start up to 10:05 through the same engine. You get exactly what was written at 10:05, not later edits.
- **Editors (multi-line):** each later session continues the previous one's document, so only the latest state of each document is shown, not every intermediate copy.
- **Single-line fields:** each session is its own entry (a command, a search, a chat message), so all of them in the window are listed, in order.
- **Output:** a `text` field joining everything, plus a `sessions` list with each part's id, window title and times.

**How it avoids duplicating code:** to replay a session to a point in time, the engine needs the document the session started from. Today that's only available for sessions still open, which crash recovery uses via `context_state`. I'll store each session's starting state (text, cursor, selection) in its row. Then crash recovery and "text at T" become **the same replay function**, called with different bounds. Recovery gets simpler too. This changes the schema (v5), so your `brain.db` gets rebuilt from the log.

The raw rendering (`<Backspace>`, `<Ctrl+V>`) goes away entirely.

//! Ingest: tails the capture log into the SQLite index.
//!
//! Each [`Ingester::step`] reads a bounded batch of complete log lines starting at
//! the persisted offset. It writes everything it derives from them and the new
//! offset in **one transaction**. If the process dies before the commit, nothing
//! from the batch is visible and the next start re-reads the same bytes. If it
//! dies after the commit, the offset already covers the batch. Either way there
//! are no gaps and no duplicates.
//!
//! A step derives log checkpoints (seek points for `query text`) and feeds
//! every event to the [`Sessions`] engine, which opens, updates and closes
//! writing sessions and their reconstructed text in the same transaction.
//! If a step fails, the engine's in-memory state may be ahead of the
//! database, so it is rebuilt from the database and the log
//! ([`Sessions::recover`]) before the next attempt.

    pub lines: usize,

}

* **Capture** reads keyboards directly from the kernel (evdev), passively, and
  resolves each key to the character the app receives with libxkbcommon and
  the user's real layouts. Focus (app id and window title) comes from a KWin
  script calling back over D-Bus. Every event is one JSON line appended to
  `events.jsonl`.
* **Ingest** (a thread in the same process) tails the log about once a
  second. In one SQLite transaction per batch it writes log checkpoints,
  opens, updates and closes writing sessions, reconstructs their text, and
  advances the log offset. The log is the ground truth; the database is
  derived from it and can be rebuilt from it.

Once a second, the ingest thread syncs the log and runs steps of at most 5,000
lines until it has caught up. **Each step is one SQLite transaction** that
holds everything derived from those lines and the new log offset:

1. read complete lines from `ingest_state.log_offset`;
2. write a log checkpoint at most every 5 s of log time;
3. feed each event to the session engine (section 4);
4. once caught up, close sessions idle on the wall clock, write finished tier
   2 results, refresh the live text of open sessions;
5. store the new offset and commit.
| with sessions open | open sessions are rebuilt from the database and their events replayed from the log (section 4.5); the restart's `start` event then closes them |

## Assistant  <sub>2026-11-17T09:52:09.797Z</sub>

`query text` now returns reconstructed text, built with the same engine as `search` and crash recovery; no reconstruction code is duplicated. Everything is pushed (`eb0da31`, then the `ai-logs/` refresh `fe7c229`).

**What it returns:** the app's text as it stood at the end of the window.
- **A session that ended inside the window** contributes its stored final text.
- **A session still running at the end of the window** is replayed from the log up to that moment, so `--at 11:50:28` shows exactly what was there then, not later edits. In the live check, the editor queried at "4 s ago" showed its text up to that point, with the typo the typist had corrected already gone.
- **Editors:** each later session continues the previous one's document, so only the latest state of each document is shown.
- **Single-line fields** (commands, searches, messages) are each listed in order. Konsole gave `git status`, `cargo test`, `ls -la`, `git status`.
- **Output:** `text` joins the parts one per line. A new `sessions` list gives each part's id, window, start and end. `ended_at` is `null` if the session was still running at the end of the window.

**How duplication was avoided:** each session row now stores the document it started from (text, cursor, selection). Crash recovery's replay became one shared function that works two ways:
- **Crash recovery:** all open sessions, up to what has been ingested.
- **`text`:** one session, up to a point in time.

Recovery got simpler as a side effect: it no longer depends on `context_state`.

**Removed, since nothing uses it any more:**
- The raw renderer (`<Backspace>`, `<Ctrl+V>`).
- The log bookmarks (`log_checkpoints`). Only the raw `text` read the log by time.
- The clock-jump limitation, which only affected that read.

**Tests:**
- **New unit test:** a session part-way through and at its end, a later session continuing a document, and a still-open session.
- **CLI tests rewritten for the new output:**
  - "secret", typed and deleted, doesn't appear.
  - Two Kate sessions give only the final document.
  - `--at` in the middle of a running session gives the partial text.
  - Commands, pastes, local times, full app ids and the error cases.
- **Results:** 119 unit tests, crash safety, `query_cli` and `perf_budget` all pass, and clippy is clean.

**Docs:** README, PLAN.md, CLAUDE.md and the `text` help all describe the new behavior, with the earlier raw output noted as changed at your request.

The schema is now version 5, so rebuild once:
```
! rm ~/brain-data/brain.db && make
```

Here's the plan. Nothing else in the design changes: the window, the bookmarks, reading the log, app resolution, the JSON shape and the schema all stay as they are. Only the last step, turning the selected events into text, changes, and it reuses the existing tier 0/1 code.

**What stays exactly as it is** (`query::text` in `src/query.rs`):
1. Work out the window from the time flags.
2. Find the starting point in the log from the bookmarks.
3. Read the log forward. Keep the typing events (keys and pastes) inside the window whose app matches, and resolve `--app` to one full id.
4. Output `{app, at, from, to, text}`. Same fields, local times.

**What changes: step 5, the text.** `render_key` is deleted. The chosen app's events, in log order, go through the same tier 0/1 pieces the session engine uses, called directly with no copies:
- `apps::classify(app)` picks the app class (terminal, browser, editor…), and `apps::normalize_window(title)` gives the window's key.
- `editor::action(class, key, mods)` turns each key into an action.
- `FieldEditor::apply` applies it to a `TextBuffer`.
- `FieldEditor::paste` inserts pasted text.
- `editor::key_suppresses_paste` drops the paste after a plain Ctrl+V in a terminal.

**Putting it together:**
- **One text field per window title** (normalized), so typing in two Kate documents isn't merged.
- **An action that ends the field** (Enter in a terminal or browser, Ctrl+C at a prompt, Tab or Ctrl+L in a browser) closes that field's text as one part, and the next keys start a new empty field. That's the same thing the session engine does.
- **Shell history (Up/Down)** recalls the lines already submitted earlier in the same window of the query, so no database lookup is needed.
- **The output `text`** is the parts in order (closed fields when they close, open fields at the end of the window), one per line. Blank parts are dropped.

**Example:** the keys `t h e ␣ c a t ␣ s a t ␣ s e c r e t` followed by 7 × Backspace give `"the cat sat"`, not `the cat sat secret<Backspace>×7`. In Konsole, `git status⏎ls⏎` gives `"git status\nls"`.

**Limits of doing it only on the window's keys** (to be documented):
- The text starts empty at the window's start, because text typed before the window isn't known. A Backspace or Ctrl+A that reaches into earlier text has nothing to act on.
- Cursor moves made with the mouse aren't seen, as everywhere else.
- A window whose title changes because of the typing (a new VS Code file) would be split into several fields. Following those renames is session-engine logic, and I'd rather not duplicate it here.

/// The raw typed stream of one app over the window: every key as captured,
/// with no editing applied (see [`render_key`]), and pasted text inline.
/// `app` may be part of the app id; see [`resolve_app`].
pub fn text(dir: &DataDir, app: &str, flags: &TimeFlags, now: Millis) -> Result<TextOutput> {
    let w = resolve(flags, Command::Text, now)?;
    let (from, to) = (w.from.unwrap_or(Millis::MIN), w.to.unwrap_or(now));
    let conn = store::open_reader(&dir.db_path())?;
    let start = store::seek_offset_before(&conn, &timefmt::format_ms(from))?;
    let needle = app.to_lowercase();
    let mut known: Vec<String> = conn
        .prepare("SELECT DISTINCT app FROM sessions")?
        .query_map([], |r| r.get(0))?
        .collect::<rusqlite::Result<_>>()?;
    drop(conn);
    // Events of every app matching `app` in the window, in log order; the
    // app is resolved once the window's apps are known too.
    let mut matching: Vec<(String, EventKind)> = Vec::new();
    if dir.log_path().exists() {
        let mut reader = LogReader::open(&dir.log_path(), start)?;
        while let Some(line) = reader.next_line()? {
            let Some(ev) = line.event else { continue };
            if ev.ts > to.saturating_add(CLOCK_SLACK_MS) {
                break;
            }
            let typed = matches!(ev.kind, EventKind::Key { .. } | EventKind::Paste { .. });
            if typed && ev.ts >= from && ev.ts <= to && ev.app.to_lowercase().contains(&needle) {
                if !known.contains(&ev.app) {
                    known.push(ev.app.clone());
                }
                matching.push((ev.app, ev.kind));
            }
        }
    }
```

## Query

Both commands run while `brain run` is capturing and print JSON. Errors go
to stderr with a non-zero exit code.

```sh
brain query search "migration blocked" [--app A] [--from T] [--to T] [--at T] [--limit N]
brain query text --app A [--from T] [--to T] [--at T]
```

* **`search`**: sessions whose text contains *every* word, anywhere inside
  a word, in any case (`run` finds "rerun", `בית` finds "בבית"), newest
  first (default limit 20). Open sessions are included with what has been
  typed so far (`ended_at: null`).
* **`text`**: what was typed into the app during the window,
  **reconstructed**: the window's keys and pastes, per window title, run
  through the app's tier 0/1 rules (Backspace, selections, undo, Enter
  submitting a shell line, …), each window starting empty at the window's
  start. Sessions play no part: a document edited in several sessions is one
  text. `windows` lists each window's text, ordered by its first keystroke;
  `text` joins them one per line. Edits reaching into text typed before the
  window (Backspace past its start, Ctrl+A) only affect what was typed
  inside it.
* **`--app A`** can be part of the app id, ignoring case (`--app chrome`
  finds `google-chrome`). `search` keeps every app that matches. `text`
  resolves `A` to one app and reports its full id (`"app": "google-chrome"`):
  an exact match wins, otherwise the one id that contains `A`; if several do,
  or none, it is an error that lists them, so text of different apps is
  never mixed.

**Time flags** (both commands): `--at T` is the 10 minutes ending at T;
`--from T` alone runs to now; `--from` and `--to` together are an explicit
window. `--to T` alone means the 10 minutes ending at T for `text`, and
everything up to T for `search`. With no flags, `text` covers the last 10
minutes and `search` all time. T can be:

| relative to now | `-30s`, `-15m`, `-2h`, `-1d`, `-1h30m`, `now` |

## 6. Query semantics

(`src/query.rs`)

- **`brain query search "<words>" [--app A] [--from T] [--to T] [--at T]
  [--limit N]`**: sessions whose text contains every word (substrings, any
  case), newest first, default limit 20, with a snippet around the first
  match. Open sessions are included with their live text and
  `ended_at: null`. A session is in a time window if it overlaps it.
- **`brain query text --app A [--from T] [--to T] [--at T]`**: what was typed
  into the app during the window, reconstructed. The window's key and paste
  events (read from the log, section 5.5) are split per window title and
  each window's events run, from an empty text, through the app's tier 0/1
  adapter: the same `editor::action` and `FieldEditor` the session engine
  uses, without sessions. A submit in a single-line field (Enter at a shell
  prompt) keeps the line and continues on a fresh one; Up recalls lines
  submitted earlier in the window. Output: `windows` (each window's text,
  by first keystroke) and `text` (them joined, one per line). *Differs from
  the design*, where `text` was the raw keystroke stream; the owner changed
  it.
- **`--app A`** can be part of an app id, ignoring case. `search` keeps
  every matching app; `text` resolves it to one full id (exact match first,
  else the single id containing it; ambiguous or unknown is an error) and
  reports that id.
- **Windows**: `--at T` is the 10 minutes ending at T; `--from` alone runs to
  now; `--from` and `--to` together are explicit; `--to` alone is the 10
  minutes ending at T for `text` and everything up to T for `search`; no
  flags means the last 10 minutes for `text` and all time for `search`.
- **Times**: relative (`-30s`, `-15m`, `-2h`, `-1d`, `-1h30m`, `now`), local
  (`2026-11-16 14:00`, a date, or a time of day meaning today; DST folds
  take the earlier instant, DST gaps are an error), or RFC 3339 with a zone.
  Output times are local with their offset (RFC 3339), and the resolved
  window is echoed; the log and the database store UTC.
- Errors (empty query, bad time, empty window, `--at` with `--from`/`--to`,
  missing data directory) go to stderr with a non-zero exit code.

## 7. Resource budget
```

The range's key and\n  paste events (read from the log, section 5.5) are split per app window\n  (window title) and each app window's events run, from an empty text,\n  through the app's tier 0/1 adapter: the same `editor::action` and\n  `FieldEditor` the session engine uses, without sessions. <details><summary>Tool result</summary>

```
### 5.5 Log checkpoints

`query text` must read the keys of a time window from the log without
scanning it from the start. Each checkpoint says "the event at this byte has
this timestamp". Because the log is written in time order, starting at the
latest checkpoint at or before the window misses nothing, and reads at most
5 s of log before the window; reading stops 60 s of log after it. Per-app
checkpoints would not save work, since the log interleaves apps and the
window has to be read anyway. Clock steps backwards are discussed in section
10.

## 6. Query semantics
## 9. Testing strategy

- **Unit tests** (about 120, `cargo test`): key resolution and layouts,
  repeat synthesis (including a 300-scenario stress test against an
  independent model, with random early and late wakeups), the recorder, the
  log's torn-tail repair, schema and search, ingest, the tier 0 buffer and
  tier 1 rules, title normalization and renames, every session rule, crash
  recovery after every line, time parsing and query windows.
- **Integration tests run by default**: `crash_safety` (25 `kill -9`s under
  load, compared with a clean rebuild), `query_cli` (the binary's JSON
  output, search semantics through the CLI, time windows, raw text, errors,
  and thousands of queries while `run` writes), `perf_budget` (CPU and
  memory budget).
- **Opt-in tests against real software**: `repeat_e2e` and
  `real_keyboard_e2e` type through a uinput keyboard into real Kate windows
  and compare Kate's saved files with brain (held-key repeats, Hebrew via
  Alt+Shift, focus moving between windows, keyboard unplug/replug);
  `vscode_replay` and `tier2_e2e` drive real VS Code.
- **Manual, once**: sleep/wake through a real suspend, screen lock and
  unlock, the systemd service (start, restart after `kill -9`, clean stop).

## 10. Limitations and future work
```

## Decisions already made by the owner — do not re-litigate

- `brain query text` reconstructs "stupidly": the keys typed in the time
  window, per app and window title, run through the tier 0/1 adapters from
  an empty text (no sessions involved); output `windows` + joined `text`.
  It replaced the earlier raw-keystroke output at the owner's request.
  Window: default last 10 min,
  `--at T` = 10-min window ending at T, or `--from/--to`. Times accept
  relative (`-2h`), local and RFC 3339 forms. `--app` may be part of the id;
  `text` resolves it to exactly one app and reports the full id.
- Sessions: keyed by (app, normalized window title); close after 30 s idle
  in that context or on Enter in single-line contexts; focus loss alone
  never closes a session; a title change of the typed window (a `renamed`
  focus event) shortly after a keystroke keeps the session.
- The mouse is not captured (owner's call): cursor moves made with the mouse
  are a documented limitation, not something to work around.
- Reconstruction tiers: 0 = generic buffer replay, 1 = per-app rules,
  2 = VS Code real-app replay, **opt-in** via `brain run --vscode-replay`,
  falling back to tier 0. Sessions, reconstruction and indexing are built
  before `brain query` (owner's call, changing the original stage order).
- Search is substring matching (FTS5 trigram, case- and accent-insensitive),
  not the design's porter stemming: `run` must find "rerun", `בית` "בבית".
- Sessions and their text must stay a pure function of the log: the crash
  test compares the live index with a fresh rebuild.
- Work went through stages (capture with sessions and indexing, query,
  end-to-end verification), each approved by the owner. Keep the habit for
  new work: build, run, test it yourself, report, then **stop and wait for
  explicit approval** before starting the next piece.
